title: Learning to Love Edge Cases in Formative Math Assessment: Using the AMMORE Dataset and Chain-of-Thought Prompting to Improve Grading Accuracy
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically grading open-response math answers in educational settings, especially difficult cases where rule-based systems fail to recognize mathematically correct but unusually formatted student responses. The authors introduce AMMORE, a new dataset of more than 53,000 open-response math answers collected from the Rori WhatsApp-based math tutor used by students in several African countries. The dataset includes human-reviewed ground-truth labels, lesson metadata, student identifiers, and demographic fields, making it useful for studying real-world math response patterns and grading behavior.

The paper evaluates several grading strategies on a hard subset of the dataset: naive string matching, text processing, GPT-4o zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, and a hybrid text-processing-plus-LLM approach. The experiments are not an intervention study with students; rather, they are offline model-evaluation experiments comparing automated predictions against human labels. A second analysis examines how differences in grading accuracy affect downstream Bayesian Knowledge Tracing estimates of student mastery.

The studied population consists of at-home users of Rori, mostly students in grades 6 to 9 in West Africa, with the dataset spanning middle-school and some high-school grade levels. The main finding is that chain-of-thought prompting produced the best grading performance among the tested LLM approaches, reducing misclassification relative to simple rule-based grading, though it was slower and sometimes inconsistent. The authors conclude that LLMs can improve grading of open-ended math answers and may support broader use of open-response formative assessment, but they also note that the work is limited to offline evaluation and does not demonstrate learning gains for students.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study, but it is not an RCT or causal evaluation of student learning outcomes. It is best classified as a comparative/technical validation study of LLM grading and downstream mastery modeling, with no direct treatment assignment to students.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are practically meaningful for grading quality and mastery estimation, including 0.97 accuracy and a reduction in mastery misclassification from 6.9% to 2.6%. However, the paper does not show direct learning gains, so impact is modest and primarily operational/instrumental rather than instructional.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based automatic short-answer grading of middle-school math open responses, including chain-of-thought prompting to classify student answers as correct or wrong and improve grading accuracy for formative assessment.
Bayesian Knowledge Tracing applied to graded lesson responses to estimate student mastery and demonstrate how grading accuracy changes ITS student modeling outputs.
A WhatsApp-based AI math tutor (Rori) that collected the student response data used in the paper, though the paper evaluates grading and mastery estimation rather than tutoring dialogue itself.

finding.finding_summary: Across 4,463 difficult-to-grade math responses, GPT-4o chain-of-thought grading achieved 0.97 accuracy and improved edge-case grading over string matching (0.79 accuracy) and zero-shot prompting (0.94). The paper argues this could reduce educator workload by enabling reliable automated grading of open-response math questions, with chain-of-thought taking 2.79 seconds on average versus 0.006 seconds for text processing and 0.68-0.73 seconds for zero-/few-shot prompting.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy, precision/recall/F1, linear weighted kappa, and latency for automated grading of student math responses
finding.study_size: n=4,463 (grading experiment); n=100 for repeated-run reliability sub-study

finding.finding_summary: Improved grading accuracy changed downstream mastery estimation in a Bayesian Knowledge Tracing model. Using human labels as the gold standard, naive string matching misestimated mastery status for 6.9% of students (165/2,388), while GPT-4o chain-of-thought reduced this to 2.6% (61/2,388), indicating substantially better mathematical mastery inference from the same student work.
finding.measure: BKT-based lesson mastery estimates and misclassification rate of mastery status across completed math lessons
